title: Vertebrates move onto land
summary: About 375 million years ago, in the Late Devonian, Tiktaalik lived in what is now Arctic Canada. Found on Ellesmere Island, this crocodile-like creature had the internal skeleton of an arm, with elbows and wrists, but fins instead of clear fingers. Researchers describe it as a link between fish and land animals, and study it to understand the water-to-land transition of limbed vertebrates.

uncertainty.note: Dated by transitional elpistostegalian and early tetrapod fossils from the Late Devonian, notably Tiktaalik (~375 Ma) and East Greenland tetrapods Acanthostega and Ichthyostega (~365 Ma).

where.modern_name: Ellesmere Island, Nunavut, Canada (where Tiktaalik was found)
where.historical_name: Tropical river delta system on the southern margin of Laurussia near the Devonian equator (no human political geography existed)

paleo.not_applicable: Late Devonian equatorial river and floodplain ecosystems across Euramerica/Laurussia.

importance.justification: The vertebrate transition from water to land gave rise to tetrapods, founding all terrestrial amphibians, reptiles, dinosaurs, birds, and mammals.

related.because: The greening of continents by early land plants created the terrestrial vegetation, soils, and invertebrate prey bases required for vertebrate terrestrialization.
